medical.title: Ultrasound imaging without the goop: A gel-free patch shows promise
medical.summary: Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology's Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care project (SMART WITEC) have developed a dry and stretchy material that could eliminate the need for a wet and sticky gel in ultrasound imaging.

medical.title: Scientists find the brain's blueprint for spoken words
medical.summary: A new discovery by scientists at UC San Francisco rewrites our understanding of how the human brain processes speech, challenging the century-old view that understanding and producing speech are handled by separate systems. It also resolves a longstanding paradox: Why can injury to a brain region that is critical for speech comprehension also impair the ability to produce words?

medical.title: Low back pain patients carry similar abdominal muscle mass to others, study finds
medical.summary: People with low back pain have about the same amount of abdominal muscle as people without it, but a lower ratio of abdominal muscle to fat, according to a new study published Nov. 19 in the journal PLOS Digital Health by Kathryn Marusich of Stanford University, U.S., and colleagues.

medical.title: Army blast in Iowa could spread toxic lead dust up to 100 miles
medical.summary: The U.S. Army plans to blow up unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa on Friday, a blast that could carry toxic lead dust up to 100 miles (161 kilometers).

medical.title: A shared molecular weakness in glioblastoma tumor cells may offer a new treatment target
medical.summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a shared molecular trait in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer in adults. It resembles one used by immature cells during brain development and may reveal a target for future treatments.

medical.title: Lingering CAR T cells may be the cause of serious gut complication after myeloma therapy
medical.summary: Patients with multiple myeloma who developed a serious gastrointestinal side effect after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy had significantly more CAR T cells persisting in their bloodstream, according to new research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: Little-known protein may help protect spinal disks from aging
medical.summary: University of Utah researchers have characterized a protein that may help protect spinal disks from age-related damage, pointing to a possible direction for future back pain treatments. Using CRISPR to target ZNF865, also known as BLST, in human cells and mouse and rat models, the interdisciplinary team showed how increasing or decreasing BLST levels affected spinal disk health.

medical.title: Smart floss can measure blood sugar and inflammation markers
medical.summary: While the biological link between oral health and whole-body wellness has long been recognized, medicine has lacked practical tools to monitor both at home. To bridge this gap, an interdisciplinary research team led by The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) has developed an innovative gingival fluid device (GFD) featuring a disposable "Smart Floss" with a microfluidic channel and sensor array built directly inside.

medical.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture—here's how food scientists manufacture it
medical.summary: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

medical.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
medical.summary: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.

medical.title: A potential pathway to reversing liver fibrosis targets specialized immune cells
medical.summary: A new study by Western University researchers has identified a potential pathway to reversing liver fibrosis, a condition that can progress to life-threatening liver disease. Published in Science Advances, the findings demonstrate how specialized immune cells, known as mucosa-associated invariant T cells (MAIT cells), contribute to liver scarring—and how targeting them could help mitigate or reverse the damage.

medical.title: Novel CAR-T platform uses radiation-activated switch to destroy tumors more effectively
medical.summary: Engineering patients' own immune cells to find and destroy cancer using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of blood cancers. However, its use is limited in solid tumors because the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment prevents CAR T-cell entry into the tumor and causes cells that enter to become exhausted.

medical.title: Traffic noise linked to increased risk of type 2 diabetes
medical.summary: Long-term exposure to noise from road traffic and trains is linked to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, even at relatively low noise levels. This is shown in a large Scandinavian study involving researchers at the Institute of Environmental Medicine (IMM) at Karolinska Institutet, published in the journal Environmental Health Perspectives.

medical.title: Over a quarter of American adults negatively affected by health misinformation
medical.summary: More than a quarter of adults in the United States say they or a family member have been negatively affected by public health misinformation, and about 70% consider it a serious problem, according to a new study by New Mexico State University researchers.

medical.title: Children exposed to more radiation from medical scans may face higher brain tumor risk
medical.summary: A new large study led by UC Davis and UC San Francisco researchers has found that higher cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging during childhood is linked to a greater brain tumor risk in children and adolescents. Brain tumors are the second most common childhood cancers and are the leading cause of cancer death among children and adolescents.

medical.title: Engineered mice mimic rare human movement disorder in weeks rather than decades
medical.summary: Through "genome writing," inserting a large swath of human genetic material linked to a rare disease called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a research team created living mice with an accurate but accelerated version of the genetic condition, a new study shows.

medical.title: Can a small DNA fix protect against Parkinson's disease?
medical.summary: In 2021, researchers at Oslo University Hospital discovered that by switching off a specific gene in the roundworm C. elegans, they could protect a particular type of nerve cell from age-related degeneration. These are the same types of nerve cells that are affected in patients with Parkinson's disease.

medical.title: A protein could help isolate particles in blood that carry clues about neurons
medical.summary: Cells release tiny particles that can carry proteins and RNA from the cells that produced them. These membrane-enclosed packets, known as extracellular vesicles (EVs), are found in blood and other bodily fluids.

medical.title: Need for human oversight of AI-driven health care
medical.summary: Health professionals often help develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools for clinical care, but less is known about how they remain involved in monitoring these systems once they are in use.

medical.title: The connection between high-fat ketogenic diets and weight loss
medical.summary: Ketogenic diets have attracted enormous attention for their purported health benefits, particularly their ability to promote weight loss. Despite their popularity, studies investigating the composition of these high-fat, low-carbohydrate regimens have produced inconsistent results. Some studies have found substantial metabolic benefits, while others have found little or no improvement.

medical.title: You aren't just what you eat: Analysis shows exercise and fitness matter more for longevity
medical.summary: Everyone agrees that a healthy diet and regular exercise together are important for a healthier life. However, Glenn Gaesser, a professor at Arizona State University's College of Health Solutions, suggests that exercise outweighs diet when it comes to longevity.

medical.title: Blocking receptor signals can help treat fibrosis
medical.summary: In an investigator-initiated trial, researchers have shown that inhibiting the cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 can prevent fibrosis in the skin disease localized scleroderma. These findings could pave the way for the prevention and treatment of other fibrotic conditions. The study "Interleukin 4 receptor-α blockade in localised scleroderma: a phase II proof-of-concept study" was published in the journal Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases.

medical.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
medical.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

medical.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
medical.summary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

medical.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

science.title: Spirituality and religiosity associated with better quality of life in older adults
science.summary: Researchers Alessandra Buja and Sohail Akhtar at the University of Padova in Italy conducted a meta-analysis of studies looking at aging adults' quality of life in relation to spirituality and religiosity. Their findings, published Nov. 19 in the open-access journal PLOS Aging and Health, suggested that being religious or spiritual boosts one's view of one's life, and having faith generally confers a greater benefit than turning to it as a means of coping.

science.title: Chips smaller than rice grains wirelessly track heat during chemical reactions
science.summary: A fleck-sized chip at the bottom of a test tube can provide researchers with data for every second of a chemical reaction while it is occurring.

science.title: Cincinnati Zoo hopes a little shake will help Fiona the hippo pass a swallowed hat
science.summary: The Cincinnati Zoo's animal care team has been working for days to help its beloved hippo Fiona safely digest and pass a knit cap she swallowed.

science.title: Neutrons, death metal and a tiny prehistoric dragon: Scans reveal new horned reptile species from 156 million years ago
science.summary: An unassuming fossil discovery in Wyoming caused quite a stir: Was it a baby dinosaur, a prehistoric snake or perhaps an entirely new species? Neutron imaging at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI and the trained eye of a paleontologist eventually provided the answer: the 156-million-year-old fossil is that of a previously unknown species of reptile.

science.title: Diplomacy, humor and avoidance—what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
science.summary: Several years ago, the U.S. economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analyzed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

science.title: Newly discovered gut viruses offer clues to the origins of the smallpox virus family
science.summary: Human and animal digestive systems host vast communities of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. Some are harmful, others are beneficial, and many remain poorly understood. In a recent study, scientists found an entirely new group of viruses without even having to go anywhere near anyone's innards.

science.title: Artificial wetland near Valencia traps 36% of incoming microplastics, study finds
science.summary: The Tancat de la Pipa, an artificial wetland designed as a "green filter" for the Albufera de València, reduces microplastic pollution in the natural lagoon by 36%, according to research conducted by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering (IIAMA) at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV) and the Faculty of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Babe–Bolyai University in Romania published in the journal Applied Sciences.

science.title: New metal-organic material combines metallic conductivity with promise for light-sensing electronics
science.summary: In modern electronics and computing, finding advanced materials that can efficiently move electrical charges without losing energy remains a critical scientific challenge. While traditional metals conduct electricity exceptionally well, researchers continually seek innovative hybrid materials that combine the design flexibility of chemistry with true metallic performance.

science.title: Confirmed: Numbers tell, but language sells
science.summary: Suppose you are in charge of your firm's commuting policy and, after some research, you determine that 57% of your colleagues drive to work. How would you communicate that number to coworkers?

science.title: Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
science.summary: Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.

science.title: Mandatory minimum sentencing oftentimes means 10 more months in prison, study finds
science.summary: Racial minorities facing federal drug charges have allegations of conspiracy added to their cases at higher rates than their white counterparts, as prosecutors seek to push them over the threshold for a mandatory minimum sentence that then can be used in negotiating stiffer penalties, a new UConn study finds.

science.title: Lunar sample research yields new discoveries, revealing the history of the moon's largest impact basin
science.summary: An international research team led by geologists from the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has uncovered new evidence of how the moon's largest impact basin, the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin, formed and evolved over billions of years.

science.title: Museum specimens yield new subspecies of New Zealand bush wren decades after its extinction
science.summary: Ecosystems can buffer the impacts of climate change and humans for only so long before an ecological turning point is reached, a new study on Aotearoa New Zealand's extinct mātuhituhi—bush wren—has highlighted.

science.title: Why stopover sites are vital for migratory birds as spring arrives earlier
science.summary: Stopover sites are more than just places for migratory birds to rest and refuel. They also help birds adapt to climate change, according to research by Leiden ecologist Yali Si.

science.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
science.summary: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

science.title: Microplastics make up 1 in 100 airborne particles sampled at four Michigan schools
science.summary: One in 100 of the tiny particles hanging in the air we breathe in Michigan is a microplastic, according to a University of Michigan study. The study tested the air for microplastics in four locations across lower Michigan, all in the parking lots of K-12 schools. It found that microplastics constitute about 1% of particles found in the atmosphere.

science.title: Phantom forests: How low-integrity offsets lead to policy failure
science.summary: Australia's Safeguard Mechanism (SGM) is failing to reduce emissions and drive decarbonization in the industrial and mining sectors because of an overreliance on cheap, low-integrity offsets, according to a new report titled "Phantom Forests and the Safeguard Mechanism: How Low-integrity Offsets are Obstructing Climate Action."

science.title: Dark personality traits linked to better chance at getting a second date
science.summary: Some personalities stand out on the first date and end up being asked for a second date, but not the ones we expect. While very few people want to date people with dark traits like psychopathy and sadism, they seem to make a good first impression. Psychopathy involves traits such as manipulation, low empathy and impulsivity, while sadism involves taking pleasure in others' suffering. Yet, on a first date, these traits don't necessarily stop someone from coming across as an appealing romantic partner.

science.title: Hostility in online heat wave discussions shows signs of contagion, study suggests
science.summary: Anger and frustration can run high in online discussions about climate change. But a new study led by Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) suggests that hostility in these conversations tends to follow earlier hostility, hinting that people may pick up uncivil behavior from others.

science.title: Why fierce tropical downpours thrive in a relatively dry atmosphere
science.summary: Twenty years of weather radar observations around Darwin have helped researchers investigate a surprising feature of tropical rain: the fiercest local downpours tend to occur when the surrounding atmosphere is relatively dry.

science.title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
science.summary: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. By optimizing hydrogen concentration and gas flow rate, they achieved a phase purity of up to 99 mol%. The team also clarified the formation mechanism and identified factors that hinder synthesis. This method, published in the journal Inorganic Chemistry, provides a foundation for future research into applications in magnetic materials and catalysis.

science.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
science.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

science.title: Astronomers discover remarkable triple-star system just 28 light-years from Earth
science.summary: Astronomers have discovered a stellar system just 28 light-years from Earth that challenges our understanding of how stars live, die and interact as they evolve.

science.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
science.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

science.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
science.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: Spirituality and religiosity associated with better quality of life in older adults
mix_items.summary: Researchers Alessandra Buja and Sohail Akhtar at the University of Padova in Italy conducted a meta-analysis of studies looking at aging adults' quality of life in relation to spirituality and religiosity. Their findings, published Nov. 19 in the open-access journal PLOS Aging and Health, suggested that being religious or spiritual boosts one's view of one's life, and having faith generally confers a greater benefit than turning to it as a means of coping.

mix_items.title: Ultrasound imaging without the goop: A gel-free patch shows promise
mix_items.summary: Engineers at MIT and the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology's Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care project (SMART WITEC) have developed a dry and stretchy material that could eliminate the need for a wet and sticky gel in ultrasound imaging.

mix_items.title: Scientists find the brain's blueprint for spoken words
mix_items.summary: A new discovery by scientists at UC San Francisco rewrites our understanding of how the human brain processes speech, challenging the century-old view that understanding and producing speech are handled by separate systems. It also resolves a longstanding paradox: Why can injury to a brain region that is critical for speech comprehension also impair the ability to produce words?

mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Low back pain patients carry similar abdominal muscle mass to others, study finds
mix_items.summary: People with low back pain have about the same amount of abdominal muscle as people without it, but a lower ratio of abdominal muscle to fat, according to a new study published Nov. 19 in the journal PLOS Digital Health by Kathryn Marusich of Stanford University, U.S., and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Chips smaller than rice grains wirelessly track heat during chemical reactions
mix_items.summary: A fleck-sized chip at the bottom of a test tube can provide researchers with data for every second of a chemical reaction while it is occurring.

mix_items.title: Army blast in Iowa could spread toxic lead dust up to 100 miles
mix_items.summary: The U.S. Army plans to blow up unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa on Friday, a blast that could carry toxic lead dust up to 100 miles (161 kilometers).

mix_items.title: A shared molecular weakness in glioblastoma tumor cells may offer a new treatment target
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have identified a shared molecular trait in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer in adults. It resembles one used by immature cells during brain development and may reveal a target for future treatments.

mix_items.title: Cincinnati Zoo hopes a little shake will help Fiona the hippo pass a swallowed hat
mix_items.summary: The Cincinnati Zoo's animal care team has been working for days to help its beloved hippo Fiona safely digest and pass a knit cap she swallowed.

mix_items.title: Neutrons, death metal and a tiny prehistoric dragon: Scans reveal new horned reptile species from 156 million years ago
mix_items.summary: An unassuming fossil discovery in Wyoming caused quite a stir: Was it a baby dinosaur, a prehistoric snake or perhaps an entirely new species? Neutron imaging at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI and the trained eye of a paleontologist eventually provided the answer: the 156-million-year-old fossil is that of a previously unknown species of reptile.

mix_items.title: Lingering CAR T cells may be the cause of serious gut complication after myeloma therapy
mix_items.summary: Patients with multiple myeloma who developed a serious gastrointestinal side effect after treatment with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy had significantly more CAR T cells persisting in their bloodstream, according to new research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Diplomacy, humor and avoidance—what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
mix_items.summary: Several years ago, the U.S. economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analyzed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered gut viruses offer clues to the origins of the smallpox virus family
mix_items.summary: Human and animal digestive systems host vast communities of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. Some are harmful, others are beneficial, and many remain poorly understood. In a recent study, scientists found an entirely new group of viruses without even having to go anywhere near anyone's innards.

mix_items.title: Artificial wetland near Valencia traps 36% of incoming microplastics, study finds
mix_items.summary: The Tancat de la Pipa, an artificial wetland designed as a "green filter" for the Albufera de València, reduces microplastic pollution in the natural lagoon by 36%, according to research conducted by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering (IIAMA) at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV) and the Faculty of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Babe–Bolyai University in Romania published in the journal Applied Sciences.

mix_items.title: Little-known protein may help protect spinal disks from aging
mix_items.summary: University of Utah researchers have characterized a protein that may help protect spinal disks from age-related damage, pointing to a possible direction for future back pain treatments. Using CRISPR to target ZNF865, also known as BLST, in human cells and mouse and rat models, the interdisciplinary team showed how increasing or decreasing BLST levels affected spinal disk health.

mix_items.title: Smart floss can measure blood sugar and inflammation markers
mix_items.summary: While the biological link between oral health and whole-body wellness has long been recognized, medicine has lacked practical tools to monitor both at home. To bridge this gap, an interdisciplinary research team led by The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) has developed an innovative gingival fluid device (GFD) featuring a disposable "Smart Floss" with a microfluidic channel and sensor array built directly inside.

mix_items.title: New metal-organic material combines metallic conductivity with promise for light-sensing electronics
mix_items.summary: In modern electronics and computing, finding advanced materials that can efficiently move electrical charges without losing energy remains a critical scientific challenge. While traditional metals conduct electricity exceptionally well, researchers continually seek innovative hybrid materials that combine the design flexibility of chemistry with true metallic performance.

mix_items.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture—here's how food scientists manufacture it
mix_items.summary: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

mix_items.title: Confirmed: Numbers tell, but language sells
mix_items.summary: Suppose you are in charge of your firm's commuting policy and, after some research, you determine that 57% of your colleagues drive to work. How would you communicate that number to coworkers?

mix_items.title: Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
mix_items.summary: Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.

mix_items.title: Mandatory minimum sentencing oftentimes means 10 more months in prison, study finds
mix_items.summary: Racial minorities facing federal drug charges have allegations of conspiracy added to their cases at higher rates than their white counterparts, as prosecutors seek to push them over the threshold for a mandatory minimum sentence that then can be used in negotiating stiffer penalties, a new UConn study finds.

mix_items.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
mix_items.summary: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.

mix_items.title: Lunar sample research yields new discoveries, revealing the history of the moon's largest impact basin
mix_items.summary: An international research team led by geologists from the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has uncovered new evidence of how the moon's largest impact basin, the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin, formed and evolved over billions of years.

mix_items.title: A potential pathway to reversing liver fibrosis targets specialized immune cells
mix_items.summary: A new study by Western University researchers has identified a potential pathway to reversing liver fibrosis, a condition that can progress to life-threatening liver disease. Published in Science Advances, the findings demonstrate how specialized immune cells, known as mucosa-associated invariant T cells (MAIT cells), contribute to liver scarring—and how targeting them could help mitigate or reverse the damage.

mix_items.title: Museum specimens yield new subspecies of New Zealand bush wren decades after its extinction
mix_items.summary: Ecosystems can buffer the impacts of climate change and humans for only so long before an ecological turning point is reached, a new study on Aotearoa New Zealand's extinct mātuhituhi—bush wren—has highlighted.

mix_items.title: Why stopover sites are vital for migratory birds as spring arrives earlier
mix_items.summary: Stopover sites are more than just places for migratory birds to rest and refuel. They also help birds adapt to climate change, according to research by Leiden ecologist Yali Si.

mix_items.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
mix_items.summary: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

mix_items.title: Novel CAR-T platform uses radiation-activated switch to destroy tumors more effectively
mix_items.summary: Engineering patients' own immune cells to find and destroy cancer using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of blood cancers. However, its use is limited in solid tumors because the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment prevents CAR T-cell entry into the tumor and causes cells that enter to become exhausted.

mix_items.title: Traffic noise linked to increased risk of type 2 diabetes
mix_items.summary: Long-term exposure to noise from road traffic and trains is linked to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, even at relatively low noise levels. This is shown in a large Scandinavian study involving researchers at the Institute of Environmental Medicine (IMM) at Karolinska Institutet, published in the journal Environmental Health Perspectives.

mix_items.title: Microplastics make up 1 in 100 airborne particles sampled at four Michigan schools
mix_items.summary: One in 100 of the tiny particles hanging in the air we breathe in Michigan is a microplastic, according to a University of Michigan study. The study tested the air for microplastics in four locations across lower Michigan, all in the parking lots of K-12 schools. It found that microplastics constitute about 1% of particles found in the atmosphere.

mix_items.title: Over a quarter of American adults negatively affected by health misinformation
mix_items.summary: More than a quarter of adults in the United States say they or a family member have been negatively affected by public health misinformation, and about 70% consider it a serious problem, according to a new study by New Mexico State University researchers.

mix_items.title: Phantom forests: How low-integrity offsets lead to policy failure
mix_items.summary: Australia's Safeguard Mechanism (SGM) is failing to reduce emissions and drive decarbonization in the industrial and mining sectors because of an overreliance on cheap, low-integrity offsets, according to a new report titled "Phantom Forests and the Safeguard Mechanism: How Low-integrity Offsets are Obstructing Climate Action."

mix_items.title: Children exposed to more radiation from medical scans may face higher brain tumor risk
mix_items.summary: A new large study led by UC Davis and UC San Francisco researchers has found that higher cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging during childhood is linked to a greater brain tumor risk in children and adolescents. Brain tumors are the second most common childhood cancers and are the leading cause of cancer death among children and adolescents.

mix_items.title: Engineered mice mimic rare human movement disorder in weeks rather than decades
mix_items.summary: Through "genome writing," inserting a large swath of human genetic material linked to a rare disease called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a research team created living mice with an accurate but accelerated version of the genetic condition, a new study shows.

mix_items.title: Dark personality traits linked to better chance at getting a second date
mix_items.summary: Some personalities stand out on the first date and end up being asked for a second date, but not the ones we expect. While very few people want to date people with dark traits like psychopathy and sadism, they seem to make a good first impression. Psychopathy involves traits such as manipulation, low empathy and impulsivity, while sadism involves taking pleasure in others' suffering. Yet, on a first date, these traits don't necessarily stop someone from coming across as an appealing romantic partner.

mix_items.title: Hostility in online heat wave discussions shows signs of contagion, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Anger and frustration can run high in online discussions about climate change. But a new study led by Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) suggests that hostility in these conversations tends to follow earlier hostility, hinting that people may pick up uncivil behavior from others.

mix_items.title: Can a small DNA fix protect against Parkinson's disease?
mix_items.summary: In 2021, researchers at Oslo University Hospital discovered that by switching off a specific gene in the roundworm C. elegans, they could protect a particular type of nerve cell from age-related degeneration. These are the same types of nerve cells that are affected in patients with Parkinson's disease.

mix_items.title: Why fierce tropical downpours thrive in a relatively dry atmosphere
mix_items.summary: Twenty years of weather radar observations around Darwin have helped researchers investigate a surprising feature of tropical rain: the fiercest local downpours tend to occur when the surrounding atmosphere is relatively dry.

mix_items.title: A protein could help isolate particles in blood that carry clues about neurons
mix_items.summary: Cells release tiny particles that can carry proteins and RNA from the cells that produced them. These membrane-enclosed packets, known as extracellular vesicles (EVs), are found in blood and other bodily fluids.

mix_items.title: Need for human oversight of AI-driven health care
mix_items.summary: Health professionals often help develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools for clinical care, but less is known about how they remain involved in monitoring these systems once they are in use.

mix_items.title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
mix_items.summary: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. By optimizing hydrogen concentration and gas flow rate, they achieved a phase purity of up to 99 mol%. The team also clarified the formation mechanism and identified factors that hinder synthesis. This method, published in the journal Inorganic Chemistry, provides a foundation for future research into applications in magnetic materials and catalysis.

mix_items.title: The connection between high-fat ketogenic diets and weight loss
mix_items.summary: Ketogenic diets have attracted enormous attention for their purported health benefits, particularly their ability to promote weight loss. Despite their popularity, studies investigating the composition of these high-fat, low-carbohydrate regimens have produced inconsistent results. Some studies have found substantial metabolic benefits, while others have found little or no improvement.

mix_items.title: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe
mix_items.summary: LONDON — On Nov. 10, Mongabay went to the site of the annual meeting of the body that regulates fishing in the northeastern Atlantic, where a little-known geopolitical dispute over marine resources was playing out behind closed doors. The North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC), a multilateral body, governs the fishing of three major stocks of fish […]

mix_items.title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
mix_items.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

mix_items.title: Astronomers discover remarkable triple-star system just 28 light-years from Earth
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have discovered a stellar system just 28 light-years from Earth that challenges our understanding of how stars live, die and interact as they evolve.

mix_items.title: You aren't just what you eat: Analysis shows exercise and fitness matter more for longevity
mix_items.summary: Everyone agrees that a healthy diet and regular exercise together are important for a healthier life. However, Glenn Gaesser, a professor at Arizona State University's College of Health Solutions, suggests that exercise outweighs diet when it comes to longevity.

mix_items.title: Blocking receptor signals can help treat fibrosis
mix_items.summary: In an investigator-initiated trial, researchers have shown that inhibiting the cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 can prevent fibrosis in the skin disease localized scleroderma. These findings could pave the way for the prevention and treatment of other fibrotic conditions. The study "Interleukin 4 receptor-α blockade in localised scleroderma: a phase II proof-of-concept study" was published in the journal Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases.

mix_items.title: How one tiny island made conservation work
mix_items.summary: Out in the Bristol Channel, nestled between Wales and England, the rugged island of Lundy is one of the UK’s most pioneering conservation stories. Watch the full story.

mix_items.title: Central-north Amazonia has experienced an ‘alarming’ increase in temperatures: Study
mix_items.summary: A small team of scientists was counting plants for a forest census near Manaus in northern Brazil when fire season started in October 2023. Some days the smoke was too thick to see; on other days it was too hot to wear conventional masks, so Aretha Guimarães, a biologist with Brazil’s National Institute of Amazonian […]

mix_items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
mix_items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

mix_items.title: Threatened species make up half of shark catches at Indonesian fishing port, study finds
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — In Muncar, a busy fishing port on the southeastern coast of Indonesia’s East Java province, sharks can fetch as much as 1.5 million rupiah each, or about $82. However, their value to fishing communities comes at a cost to conservation: Threatened species, including the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), made up a […]

mix_items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

mix_items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
mix_items.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
mix_items.summary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
